prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

The Devil’s tour of hell did not include a factory line where molten lead spilled into mouths held wide, no electric drill spiraling screws into hands and feet, nor giant pliers to lower you into simmering vats. Instead, a circle of light opened on your stuffed armchair, whose chintz orchids did not boil and change, and the Devil adjusted your new spiked antennae almost delicately, with claws curled and lacquered black, before he spread his leather wings to leap into the acid-green sky. So your head became a tv hull, a gargoyle mirror. Your doppelganger sloppy at the mouth and swollen at the joints enacted your days in sinuous slow motion, your lines delivered with a mocking sneer. Sometimes the frame froze, reversed, began again: the red eyes of a friend you cursed, your girl child cowered behind the drapes, parents alive again and puzzled by this new form. That’s why you clawed your way back to this life.

The infernal guided tour you experienced skipped the usual assembly-line torments—no boiling metal poured down open throats, no mechanical bit twisting fasteners through palms and soles, no massive tongs dunking you into bubbling cauldrons. Instead, illumination fell upon your overstuffed chair, its floral upholstery remaining static and unmelted, while Satan gently fitted you with newly grown horn-like receivers, his blackened, glossy talons moving with surprising care, before unfurling his membranous wings and launching himself into a sky the color of toxic lime.

In this way, your skull transformed into a television casing, a distorted mirror reflecting something monstrous. A twisted version of yourself—mouth slack, joints grotesquely inflated—performed the events of your existence in a viscous, drawn-out rhythm, each spoken word tinged with contemptuous ridicule. The footage would occasionally stutter to a halt, rewind, then replay: the crimson-eyed gaze of someone you'd once damned with words, your daughter hiding fearfully behind curtains, your resurrected parents staring in bewilderment at this altered shape. This is what drove you to fight your way back into existence.
outputs.L3:
# The Armchair of Endless Reflection

The Devil, it turned out, had grown tired of tradition. The molten lead had lost its luster, the drills their edge, the boiling vats their steam. These were tortures of the flesh—crude, temporary, almost merciful in their brevity. Pain, after all, could be endured. The body could scream itself hoarse and eventually go numb. No, the Devil wanted something that would linger, something that would seep into the marrow of a soul and never quite leave. So he abandoned the old catalogue of suffering entirely, favoring instead a punishment far more insidious: the mind turned against itself, forced to watch its own reflection in an unbreakable mirror.

The ritual, if it could be called that, was almost tender in its execution. There was no fire, no chains, no cavernous pit lined with the shrieks of the damned. Instead, the Devil approached with the quiet efficiency of a man performing a routine chore. He placed the person gently in their own armchair—the same worn cushions, the same familiar creak of springs—and with careful fingers, affixed a pair of spiked antennae to their skull. It was done without malice, without flourish, as though he were pinning a corsage rather than sentencing a soul. Then, without a word of explanation, he turned and departed, his silhouette dissolving into a sky the color of bruised acid, sickly green and pulsing faintly, as if the heavens themselves were nauseated by what was to come.

What came next required no further intervention. The person's own head became the instrument of their undoing. Flesh gave way to something screen-like, a flickering surface not unlike a television left in the rain, or perhaps a gargoyle's mirror—warped, reflective, cruel in its clarity. Upon this new face played a grotesque doppelganger, a twisted echo of the self, moving in slow motion through the events of days long past. Every gesture was rendered with theatrical exaggeration, every expression curdled into a sneer of mockery. The doppelganger did not simply reenact; it performed, relishing each moment with a wicked, knowing smile, as though it understood something the original never had.

The footage looped without mercy, replaying scenes that the person had perhaps hoped were buried, forgotten, forgiven by time if not by conscience. There was the friend, cursed by association, whose ruin traced back to careless words spoken in haste. There was the daughter, small and trembling, her face frozen in a fear that had been placed there by hands that should have protected her instead. There were the parents, long dead, their expressions caught in eternal bewilderment—confused not by death itself, but by the cruelty they had received from the very child they had raised with love. Each memory unspooled with excruciating patience, slow enough that no detail could be missed, no flinch of pain overlooked, no consequence left unexamined.

This was the punishment: not fire, not blade, but witness. To sit trapped within one's own armchair, head transformed into a stage for one's worst self, and watch—again and again—the damage wrought by careless cruelty. There was no escaping the screen, no diverting one's gaze, for the gaze itself had become the theater. The mind could not look away from its own face.

And yet, it was precisely this unbearable confrontation that became the catalyst for something unexpected. The horror of watching oneself inflict pain, of seeing loved ones' faces contorted in fear and confusion because of one's own hand, proved so unbearable that it ignited a desperate will to change, to return, to make amends. The person began to fight—not against the Devil, who had long since vanished into his sickly sky, but against the paralysis of guilt itself. Clawing back toward consciousness, toward life, toward the chance to rewrite even one more page of the story the screen so mercilessly replayed, they fought their way back to the living, propelled not by fear of hell's flames, but by the unbearable weight of their own reflection.
outputs.L4:
# The Devil's Television

I had always imagined hell as fire—
as pitchforks and brimstone, as chains
that bind the flesh to eternal burning.
I had prepared myself for that violence,
had steeled my nerves against the expected
theater of pain, the crude choreography
of suffering that religion promised me
since childhood, since the first warnings
whispered in dim rooms about the wages
of sin, about the reckoning that waits.

But the Devil did not reach for tongs
or blades when I arrived. He did not
gesture toward some pit of flame.
Instead, he smiled—almost gently—
and touched two fingers to my forehead,
and where my face had been, a screen
flickered into being, humming with
its own cold light, and I understood
with rising dread that I had become
the broadcast and the broadcast tower both.

He did not need to torture me himself.
He simply pressed play.

There was my friend—the one I'd cursed
in a moment of careless fury, words
I'd barely remembered saying, words
that had lodged themselves like splinters
under his skin for years after, words
that I had let fall from my mouth
like loose change, not understanding
their weight until I watched his face
crumple in that grainy replay, watched
the hurt bloom there in silence.

There was the child—was it my own,
or one I'd frightened in some careless
afternoon, some moment when my temper
rose too quickly, when my voice grew
too large for the room, too large
for the small body cowering before it?
I watched the fear take root in those eyes,
watched innocence flinch and pull away,
watched myself become the monster
that child would carry into adulthood.

There were my parents, bewildered,
standing in some doorway of memory,
their faces asking questions I never
answered, their hands reaching toward
a version of me that had already
turned away, already decided
that their confusion was not my burden,
that their hurt was collateral,
acceptable damage in my private war
against whatever I thought I was owed.

The images looped and stuttered,
distorted at the edges like a signal
losing strength, mocking in their
repetition, in their insistence
that this was who I was, that this
compilation of small cruelties
constituted a life, that no fire
could burn hotter than this recognition,
this endless mirror held up
to show me exactly what I'd done.

The Devil did not need whips.
He did not need chains or coals.
He needed only my own face
turned traitor, turned witness,
turned into the very screen
that played my sins back to me
in high definition, in merciless
color, refusing to let me look away,
refusing to let the static blur
what I had spent years trying to forget.

I do not know how long I watched.
Time bends strangely in that place,
folds in on itself like the images
folding and repeating, folding
and repeating. But at some point—
some moment I cannot quite locate—
I understood that this was not
punishment being done to me.
This was punishment I had authored,
frame by frame, moment by moment,
in every choice that led me here.

And something in that understanding
became the thing that saved me.
Not absolution—I want to be clear
that nothing absolved me in that room,
nothing erased the footage or offered
forgiveness wrapped in easy ribbon.
But recognition itself became a kind
of rope, a kind of ladder I could climb,
hand over hand, out of the pit
that was not made of fire but of truth.

I clawed my way back to life
not because I feared the flames
I had once imagined, not because
some external force decided
I deserved another chance,
but because I could not bear
to remain inside that endless loop
without at least attempting
to write a different ending,
to become someone whose future
footage might show something else—

might show the friend forgiven,
might show the child comforted,
might show the parents finally
given the answers they deserved.

Redemption, I learned, does not arrive
in the form of mercy handed down.
It arrives when we are forced to watch
ourselves clearly, without the flattering
distortions we construct to sleep at night,
without the narratives that soften
our sharpest edges. It arrives
when the screen refuses to look away,
when we become both the accused
and the reluctant witness, both
the sinner and the sin laid bare.

I came back changed—not because
I feared hell's traditional geography,
but because I had seen my own face
looking back at me, cruel and small,
and could not bear to let that be
the only broadcast, the only channel,
the only story this life would tell.
outputs.L5:
# The Devil's Instead

There's a peculiar moment that happens in decision-making, a fork in the road where we glimpse not just what we chose, but the ghost of what we didn't. Call it the devil's instead—that persistent whisper suggesting the path not taken might have led somewhere better, brighter, less burdened by the compromises of the present.

The devil, in this sense, isn't a horned figure with a pitchfork. It's subtler than that. It's the voice that surfaces during quiet moments of doubt, murmuring alternatives dressed up as certainties. *You could have taken that job instead. You could have said something different instead. You could have stayed instead of leaving, or left instead of staying.* The devil's instead thrives on hindsight's false clarity, painting unlived choices with colors reality never allows.

What makes this particular temptation so insidious is its reasonableness. It doesn't ask us to do anything wrong—it simply asks us to believe that wrong was inevitable, that right lived just one decision away, forever out of reach. This is different from ordinary regret. Regret says *I made a mistake.* The devil's instead says *there was always a better world available, and you missed it.*

Psychologists might call this counterfactual thinking, the mental exercise of imagining alternate outcomes. But there's something almost theological about how insistently it operates, how it seems to demand worship, how it can consume attention that might otherwise go toward the present moment—the one we actually inhabit, flawed and singular as it is.

Perhaps the answer isn't to silence the devil's instead entirely, but to recognize it for what it is: a story, not a certainty. The unlived life is not necessarily better; it is simply unlived, free from the friction of actual existence, and therefore able to seem perfect in ways nothing real ever can.

We build these instead-worlds because uncertainty is uncomfortable, and blaming a single choice feels better than accepting complexity. But every path carries its own devil, its own instead. There is no decision that escapes this shadow.

The task, then, isn't defeating the devil, but learning to sit beside it without following where it leads—acknowledging the whisper, and choosing, again, to stay.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal poem imagining hell not as fire and torture, but as being forced to watch a distorted replay of your own life on a screen embedded in your head.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Screening Room

There is no fire here. No pitchfork glint,
no sulfur choir singing my arrival.
Only this: a screen behind my eyes,
soldered to the bone like a second skull,
playing footage I don't remember filming.

Watch: my mother's face, but the mouth moves wrong,
saying words she never said, in a voice
that is almost hers, almost, like a song
transposed one key too high. I lean in close
to fix it, but my hands are in the theater seats,
folded, useless, applauding nothing.

The projector runs on something wet.
I can hear it behind my sternum, whirring,
grinding footage that was never shot—
a birthday party where I am the cake,
a wedding where the vows are spoken backwards,
my own face looking at me looking at it
looking back, a hallway of mirrors
built by someone who hated architecture.

Here, the punishment is not the pain.
It's the almost. It's the nearly-right.
It's watching myself wave to someone
who isn't there anymore, in a season
that never existed, wearing a coat
I never owned but recognize completely.

I try to close my eyes. There are no lids
on this kind of seeing. I try to leave.
The exit sign flickers in a language
made entirely of my own handwriting,
illegible, insistent, glowing red
like the afterimage of a life
staring too long at its own sun.

Somewhere, the credits are already rolling
for a film that hasn't started.
I recognize none of the names.
I recognize all of the names.
The screen hums on, patient as a held breath,
waiting for the scene where I finally
turn to the camera and confess
I don't remember agreeing to this,
though clearly, clearly, I bought the ticket.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a dark, imagistic piece of flash fiction where the Devil personally escorts someone to a private, psychological version of hell rather than the traditional torments.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Room

The Devil doesn't touch you. He never has to. He simply walks beside you, hands clasped behind his back like a docent at a museum, and the two of you pass through a door that wasn't there a moment ago.

"No fire," he says, almost apologetic. "That was never really the point."

The room is yours. You recognize it immediately—the apartment you had at twenty-six, the one with the water stain shaped like Portugal on the ceiling. The lamp with the burnt shade. The couch you never replaced.

"I don't understand," you say.

"You will."

He gestures to the couch, and you sit, because some part of you has always done what it's told. He sits across from you in a chair that shouldn't be there, that you don't remember owning, and folds his hands.

"Tell me about her," he says. "The one who called at 3 a.m. The one you didn't answer."

"I was asleep."

"You woke up. You saw the name. You put the phone face-down on the nightstand and went back to sleep."

"How do you—"

"I know everything you've forgotten on purpose." He says this kindly, the way a doctor delivers a diagnosis they've given a thousand times. "That's the whole apparatus here. Not punishment. Retrieval."

The phone rings. It's on the coffee table now, though it wasn't a moment ago, and you recognize the ringtone with a lurch in your chest like missing a stair.

"You don't have to answer it," the Devil says. "You didn't, before."

"What happens if I do?"

"Nothing happens. That's rather the point. It rings. It stops ringing. Then it rings again. This is not a story with an ending, and there is no lesson to learn that will make it stop. You will simply sit with the sound of it, and what you did, and did not do, for as long as it takes."

"How long does it take?"

He looks at you with something like pity, though you suspect pity is simply another tool in his kit, worn smooth from use.

"You misunderstand the architecture," he says. "There is no *it*. There is no it that ends. There is only you, and the phone, and the version of yourself that let it ring."

He stands. Straightens his cuffs.

"I'll leave you to it," he says, and the door closes behind him with no sound at all, and the phone rings, and you look at it, and outside the window it is always almost dawn, the sky the exact gray of a decision not yet made, forever arriving, never arriving, and you understand at last that hell was never a place he built.

It was a room you built yourself, one missed call at a time, and furnished so carefully that even now, staring at the phone, some old and stubborn part of you almost reaches out to answer it—

almost—

as if this time might be different.

The phone rings.

You know it won't be.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose poem about a near-death experience where the person's punishment is watching a monstrous doppelganger reenact their worst moments in front of their family.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Second Self

They tell you the light comes first, but they lie. First comes the room—your own dining room, table set for six, the good china that only came out for Christmas. Your family sits waiting, and you feel almost peaceful until you see yourself already there, standing in the doorway wearing your face like a coat two sizes too tight.

It moves the way you move, but slower, deliberate, savoring. It clears its throat with your particular hesitation before lying to your mother about where you were that November. It laughs with your laugh at the joke that cost your brother his dignity in front of everyone he loved. Your family watches this thing, this you, and they nod, they remember, they were there—of course they were there, they've always been there, in the room you never quite leave.

You try to scream *that's not me* but the words come out in its voice, borrowed and thick as syrup, and isn't that the horror—not that it's wrong, but that it's accurate. It hits every mark. It knows the exact cruelty in your silences, the specific weight of your absences. When it turns to your daughter and says the thing you said, the unforgivable thing about her mother, it says it with your exact inflection, that particular coldness you saved only for family, for the people who couldn't leave.

You want to explain context, exhaustion, the fight before the fight, the years compounding into that one sentence—but context is not admitted here. Only the moment, unadorned, played on loop while your family's faces do that thing faces do when they're deciding, again, whether to forgive you.

The doppelganger takes a bow. It has your hands, your specific scar from the bicycle when you were nine. It sits down at the table across from your mother and begins, patiently, to eat.

This is not punishment, you realize. This is inventory.

You will carry this room home with you, if you get to go home. You will set the table differently. You will learn, slowly, to become someone your monster has never met.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a literary description of hell that subverts clichés like lead, drills, and vats of acid, replacing them with a haunting scene involving a television-like transformation.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Waiting Room

Hell is not fire. Fire would be a mercy—something to scream at, something with an edge you could name.

Hell is a waiting room with fluorescent lights that never flicker, because flickering would suggest the possibility of darkness, and darkness would suggest the possibility of relief. The chairs are the color of dried blood but no one calls it that. Everyone here calls it "mauve."

In the corner, a television plays. It has always been playing. It will always be playing. The picture is slightly too bright, the way old televisions get when the tint is wrong, and everyone in the room is arranged to face it, though no one remembers choosing their seat.

The television is showing you. Not a memory—worse than that. A refinement. On the screen, you are answering the question you fumbled at that dinner party, effortlessly, wittily, and the people around that long-ago table are laughing the correct amount. On the screen, you are not saying the thing you said to your mother the last time you saw her breathing. On the screen, your hands are steady during the moment they shook.

You watch this. You have always watched this. The horror is not that it's wrong—it's that it's better. It's the you that almost happened, the you that lived in the gap between intention and execution, now given a body, a voice, a fluency you never earned.

And slowly, the thing on the screen begins to feel more real than the memory of what you actually did. The edges of the true version go soft, like a photograph left in a window. You reach for the truth and your hand closes on static.

This is the transformation: not your body twisting into something clawed and screaming, but your history revising itself in high definition, replacing you with a fluent ghost until you can no longer say, with any confidence, which one of you was the original.

The damned do not weep here. They lean forward slightly, chins tilted, the blue light flickering on their patient, forgetting faces—

waiting to see what they'll become next.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a vivid, unsettling narrative fragment about someone being shown their own sins through a warped mirror-self, ending with them fighting to return to life.
counterfactuals.output:
The mirror had been in the attic for as long as she could remember, wrapped in a sheet like something ashamed of itself. Mara pulled the cloth away without knowing why—the way you touch a bruise to confirm it still hurts.

Her reflection did not move when she did.

It stood there a half-second longer each time, watching her through the silvered glass with an expression of patient, terrible tenderness, and then it smiled. Not her smile. Wider. Full of a knowledge she didn't have.

"Let me show you," it said, though the glass didn't ripple, though no sound reached her ears so much as her bones.

The attic dissolved. She was standing in her childhood kitchen, small again, watching herself—the other self, the real one, the one still trapped behind the glass—steal coins from her mother's purse and lie about it so easily, so sweetly, that even now, decades later, some doubting animal part of her whispered *it wasn't so bad.* The mirror-self turned to her and its smile stretched further, cracking at the corners like drying mud.

Then another scene: her father in his last months, and her own voice on the phone saying *I'll come next week, I promise*, week after week after week, until there was no week left to come to. The mirror-Mara mouthed the words along with her memory, savoring them, and where its mouth split too wide she saw not teeth but rows of small dark doors.

"You buried it well," it said. "I kept it for you."

Every unkindness she'd folded into forgetting unspooled before her—not exaggerated, not embellished, just *true*, stripped of the softening gauze she'd wrapped around them for years. The mirror did not lie. That was the horror of it. It only removed the mercy.

"Stop," she said, and her voice came out as a child's.

"Why? You made me. Every year, every small cruelty, a little more of you came to live here." It lifted a hand—her hand, but longer now, the fingers jointed wrong, reaching not through the glass but *around* it, as if the glass were merely a doorway it had been courteous enough to use until now. "Come inside. You're most of the way here already."

The attic reasserted itself in jagged pieces, like a room remembering how to exist. Mara found she could not look away from her own eyes, black-mirrored, patient, so sure of their claim on her.

"No," she said, and this time her voice was hers. "I did those things. I'm not only those things."

The reflection's smile faltered—just slightly, just enough.

She thought of her father's hand in hers those last days despite her failures, thought of the moments she had shown up, imperfect and late but present, thought of every small grace she'd also folded into forgetting because shame is a hoarder and does not display its better inventory.

"I get to decide what I carry," she said, "not you."

The glass screamed—a sound like metal remembering it was once sand—and she felt the attic's cold floor bite into her knees, felt her own pulse slam against her ribs like something fighting to be let back into a body it had nearly left. She grabbed the edge of the mirror's frame and *pulled*, not away from herself, but toward the version of her that was still breathing, still capable of change, still unfinished.

Somewhere far off, she heard herself gasp—a real gasp, wet and ragged and alive—and the attic, the glass, the smile all folded into that single sound and were gone.

She woke on the floor of the room that had no mirror at all, her heart going like a fist on a door, and would not, for a long time, be able to say which side of the glass she'd been fighting to leave.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
